rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه
rows.claim: A report preserved in al-Tawḥīd has the speaker concede that healing and admission to Paradise occur when God wills, rather than when the person chooses.
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن الميمون القداح عن جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه عليهما السلام وفيه فيدخلك حيث يشاء أو حيث شئت

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā says that will is an attribute of action, and that whoever claims God has always been willing and choosing is not a monotheist.
rows.anchor: إلى سليمان بن جعفر الجعفري قال قال الرضا عليه السلام المشيئة من صفات الأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads al-Riḍā’s wording as identifying will and choice: in humans, choice describes acting knowingly, while will names that agency when action necessarily follows.
rows.anchor: تلويح إلى اتحاد الإرادة والمشيئة وهو كذلك فإن المشيئة معنى يوصف به الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine will is an attribute of action inferred from the act or its causes, not an essential attribute; saying God willed something means He did it, or prepared its causes, knowing it best.
rows.anchor: هو وصف خارج عن الذات طارئ عليه، ولذلك لا يتصف تعالى بها كأتصافه بصفاته الذاتية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If will is distinct from God's essence yet eternal, it posits an uncreated entity alongside Him and conflicts with monotheism.
rows.anchor: كان لازمه إثبات شيء أزلي غير مخلوق له معه وهو خلاف توحيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defining will as knowledge of what is best avoids the problem by reducing it to divine knowledge, but then there is no basis to count it as another attribute beyond life, knowledge, and power.
rows.anchor: ولا محذور فيه غير أن عد الإرادة على هذا صفة أخرى وراء الحياة والعلم والقدرة لا وجه له

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: Abū Dharr swore that the passage about the two disputing parties, through “God does what He wills,” was revealed about the three-on-three duel at Badr: Ḥamza, ʿUbayda, and ʿAlī against ʿUtba, Shayba, and al-Walīd.
rows.anchor: عن أبي ذر أنه كان يقسم قسما أن هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the believers’ protector who defends them from enemies, as also stated at 47:11.
rows.anchor: فهو تعالى مولاهم ووليهم الذي يدفع عنهم أعداءه كما قال ذلك بأن الله مولى الذين آمنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse institutes permission to fight rather than reporting an earlier permission; its context identifies fighting as the act being permitted.
rows.anchor: ظاهر السياق أن المراد بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading makes yuqātalūn passive: these are believers whom polytheists fight, since the polytheists sought and initiated combat.
rows.anchor: والقراءة الدائرة { يقاتلون } بفتح التاء مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bāʾ marks cause: fighting is permitted because the believers were wronged, with the next verse explaining that injustice.
rows.anchor: والباء في { بأنهم ظلموا } للسببية وفيه تعليل الإذن في القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unexpressed subject of “permission was given” magnifies the permission’s source; mentioning God's power to aid without stating its enactment signals how easy victory is for Him.
rows.anchor: وفي عدم التصريح بفاعل { أذن } تعظيم وتكبير ونظيره ما في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers were driven from their homes in Mecca by polytheist abuse, torture, and persecution that forced some to Abyssinia and others to Medina; “expelled” means compelled to leave, not physically deported.
rows.anchor: ولم يخرجوهم بحمل وتسفير بل آذوهم وبالغوا في إيذائهم وشددوا بالتعذيب والتفتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the exception as disconnected: they were expelled, but only because they said “Our Lord is God,” exposing the polytheists’ perverse treatment of truth as grounds for eviction.
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع معناه ولكن أخرجوا بسبب أن يقولوا ربنا الله

words: بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ إِلَّآ أَن يَقُولُوا۟ رَبُّنَا ٱللَّهُ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes the exception as connected, with “the right” as the excepted element: their profession of God was the only right involved; the author rejects this as contrary to the verse’s point that they had no lawful cause for expulsion.
rows.anchor: وقيل الاستثناء متصل والمستثنى منه هو الحق والمعنى أخرجوا بغير حق إلا الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes all believers by the experience of some—the emigrants—because believers form one united community; the Qur'an often attributes some members’ qualities to the whole.
rows.anchor: وهو وصف بعضهم وهم المهاجرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣawāmiʿ are taper-topped structures in mountains or wilderness where ascetics and recluses worship; biyaʿ are Jewish and Christian temples, and masājid are Muslim mosques.
rows.anchor: الصوامع جمع صومعة وهي بناء في أعلاه حدة كان يتخذ في الجبال والبراري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣalawāt refers to Jewish prayer houses, naming the place by the act performed there, as al-ṣalāt means a mosque in 4:43.
rows.anchor: والصلوات جمع صلاة وهي مصلى اليهود سمي بها تسمية للمحل باسم الحال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation derives ṣalawāt from the Aramaic or Syriac ṣlotha, meaning a place of prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي معرب صلوثا بالثاء المثلثة والقصر وهي بالعبرانية المصلى

words: وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a rationale for combat, the verse says fighting protects religious society from enemies seeking to extinguish God's light; without it, worship sites and rites would be erased.
rows.anchor: ومحصلها أن تشريع القتال إنما هو لحفظ المجتمع الديني من شر أعداء الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's pushing people against one another is broader than battle: mutual defense of life's interests is an innate social law, ultimately grounded in God.
rows.anchor: لكن المراد بدفع الله الناس بعضهم ببعض أعم من القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People are equipped with physical powers and reason to devise means of self-defense and protect the conditions of a good life; fighting is a last resort, like cautery, accepting some loss so others may live.
rows.anchor: ويشهد به تجهيز الإنسان كسائر الموجودات بأدوات وقوى تسهل له البطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship sites are singled out because they are the visible signs of religion that remind people of it and preserve its image in their minds, although religion's broader existence is at stake.
rows.anchor: لأن هذه المعابد والمعاهد هي الشعائر والأعلام الدالة على الدين المذكرة له الحافظة لصورته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic oath promises aid to those who fight in defense of divine religion; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God fulfilled it by supporting Muslim campaigns and raising the religion's name as they supported it.
rows.anchor: قسم مع تأكيد بالغ على نصره تعالى من ينصره بالقتال ذبا عن الدين الإلهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is powerful, whom none can weaken or prevent from acting, and mighty, inaccessible in His sovereignty and unmatched in dominion.
rows.anchor: إن الله لقوي لا يضعفه أحد ولا يمنعه شيء عما أراد عزيز منيع الجانب

words: وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse suggests that earlier religious laws also contained a defensive rule, though it does not explain its form.
rows.anchor: ويظهر من الآية أنه كان في الشرائع السابقة حكم دفاعي في الجمله وإن لم يبين كيفيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True blindness is blindness of insight, not loss of eyesight.
rows.anchor: ليس الأعمى من يعمى بصره ولكن الأعمى من تعمى بصيرته

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report from al-Bāqir distinguishes a prophet, who sees dreams and hears a voice without seeing the angel, from a messenger, who also sees the angel.
rows.anchor: عن زرارة عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام في حديث النبي الذي يرى في منامه ويسمع الصوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports clarify that seeing the angel means his descent, appearance to the prophet, and communication of revelation; the author had discussed related reports in his prophethood study.
rows.anchor: والمراد بمعاينة الملك على ما في غيره من الروايات نزول الملك عليه وظهوره له

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: A report with a chain the source calls sound says that during the Prophet's Meccan recitation of al-Najm, Satan put praise of the pagan goddesses on his tongue; the polytheists rejoiced and prostrated, and Gabriel later disavowed the words.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير قال قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بمكة النجم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجمع من التابعين
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes that the Gharānīq report has numerous routes from Ibn ʿAbbās and Successors and was authenticated by a group including Ibn Ḥajar.
rows.anchor: الرواية مروية بطرق عديدة عن ابن عباس وجمع من التابعين وقد صححها جماعة منهم الحافظ ابن حجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite those chains, the author rejects the report: infallibility excludes the alleged grave ignorance of reciting explicit pagan disbelief, prostrating with its hearers, repeating it to Gabriel, and needing correction by a verse that attributes such error to prophets.
rows.anchor: لكن الأدلة القطعية على عصمته صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم تكذب متنها وإن فرضت صحة سندها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The proposed defense that Satan caused a single inadvertent slip of the tongue does not fit the report's detailed sequence, and infallibility does not allow such an error.
rows.anchor: بأن ذلك كان سبقا من لسان دفعة بتصرف من الشيطان سهوا منه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Satan could place verses on the Prophet's tongue, trust in revelation would collapse: even the verse disclosing the incident could itself be Satanic and disguise further insertions.
rows.anchor: لو جاز مثل هذا التصرف من الشيطان في لسانه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بإلقاء آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, if the Gharānīq words were divine, Satan could have supplied the corrective verse and all anti-idolatry passages, destroying confidence in scripture and the prophetic mission.
rows.anchor: أو يكون حديث الغرانيق من الكلام الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage closes the sūra's call to preach by exposing shirk, summarizing the believers' duties as worship and good works, and commanding striving in God's cause.
rows.anchor: بيان الآيات تأمره صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بالدعوة وتبين أمورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mansak is a verbal noun meaning worship, as confirmed by “they perform it”; it is not a place noun, contrary to another proposed explanation.
rows.anchor: المنسك مصدر ميمي بمعنى النسك وهو العبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Each community” means successive past communities through the present one, not different peoples living together in the Prophet's time, because prophecy and its law are universal and one.
rows.anchor: والمراد بكل أمة هي الأمة بعد الأمة من الأمم الماضين حتى تنتهي إلى هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God replaced earlier rites with better ones for later communities as their intellectual development and readiness advanced, so earlier rites were abrogated for successors and cannot invalidate the Prophet's rite.
rows.anchor: بدل منسك السابقين مما هو أحسن منه في حق اللاحقين لتقدمهم في الرقي الفكري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition addresses unbelievers disputing the Prophet's rites; although they deny his authority, it is not empty, because the verse's opening gives the argument on which it rests.
rows.anchor: لكن هذا النهي لما كان معتمدا على الحجة لم يصر لغوا لا أثر له وهي صدر الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied objection is that unfamiliar Islamic rites were absent from earlier laws and thus could not be prophetic; the answer is that each community had a distinct rite, later laws superseding earlier ones.
rows.anchor: كأن الكفار من أهل الكتاب أو المشركين لما رأوا من عبادات الإسلام ما لا عهد لهم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After telling the Prophet not to heed their contention, God turns him back to his task: call people to his Lord.
rows.anchor: طب نفسا ولا تعبأ بمنازعتهم واشتغل بما أمرت به وهو الدعوة إلى ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling guidance “straight” is a rational metaphor, since straightness properly describes the path toward which guidance leads.
rows.anchor: وتوصيف الهدي بالاستقامة وهي وصف الصراط الذي إليه الهداية من المجاز العقلي

words: وَإِن جَٰدَلُوكَ فَقُلِ ٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute concerns the Prophet's differing rites and earlier laws; after explaining abrogation, he is told to leave judgment to God instead of trading arguments with them.
rows.anchor: وقد أمر صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بإرجاعهم إلى حكم الله من غير أن يشتغل بالمجادلة معهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing believers' virtues, the passage explains human creation and provision to show that God alone is Lord of humanity and all things and alone deserves worship.
rows.anchor: عقبه بشرح خلقهم وخلق ما أنعم عليهم من النعم مقرونا بتدبير أمرهم

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ glosses sulāla as what is extracted from something, like kusāḥa for what is swept away.
rows.anchor: قال في المجمع السلالة اسم لما يسل من الشيء كالكساحة اسم لما يكسح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The human” denotes the human kind, including Adam and his descendants: Adam was first formed from clay, then his offspring from a drop, as in 32:7–8; readings limited to Adam's descendants or to Adam alone are rejected.
rows.anchor: وظاهر السياق أن المراد بالإنسان هو النوع فيشمل آدم ومن دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “human” meant only Adam's descendants and their clay origin meant semen ultimately comes from earth, the next clause should say “then We created him as a drop,” paralleling the subsequent stages.
rows.anchor: لكان الظاهر أن يقال ثم خلقناه نطفة كما قيل ثم خلقنا النطفة علقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root meaning of khalq is measurement or proportioning, like measuring cloth before cutting; the human was first proportioned from earth's elements mixed with water.
rows.anchor: التقدير يقال خلقت الثوب إذا قسته لتقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuṭfa means a little water, sometimes water generally; qarār, literally a verbal noun, emphatically means the place of settlement—the womb—and makīn describes its secure holding of the drop or the drop's secure position.
rows.anchor: النطفة القليل من الماء وربما يطلق على مطلق الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stages show a change in the mode of creation: God first formed the human from clay, then made him a drop securely settled in the womb.
rows.anchor: أي بدلنا طريق خلقه من هذا إلى ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says he explained this verse's individual terms earlier in his discussion of 22:5.
rows.anchor: تقدم بيان مفردات الآية في الآية 5 من سورة الحج في الجزء السابق من الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We clothed the bones with flesh” is a subtle implied metaphor.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله { فكسونا العظام لحما } استعارة بالكناية لطيفة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib explains inshāʾ as bringing something into existence and nurturing it, as in the terms nashʾ and nashʾa.
rows.anchor: إيجاد الشيء وتربيته كما أن النشء والنشأة إحداثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing from khalq to inshāʾ marks a novel being not contained in prior matter: life, knowledge, and power have no counterpart in the drop, clot, morsel, or clothed bones, so the human self is newly brought into being.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على حدوث أمر حديث ما كان يتضمنه ولا يقارنه ما تقدمه من مادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We brought him into being” refers to the human whose bones had been clothed with flesh; he is transformed from dead, ignorant, powerless matter into a living, knowing, capable being.
rows.anchor: للإنسان المخلوق عظاما مكسوة باللحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person is the former matter insofar as it becomes human, but is not identical with that matter: its essence and properties differ, with only a union in which the person uses the body as a tool, like a writer uses a pen.
rows.anchor: فهو تلك المادة السابقة فإنها التي صارت إنسانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion links the distinction of person and body to 32:10–11: at death the human is taken, while the body is scattered in the earth.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الذي يستفاد من مثل قوله وقالوا أئذا ضللنا في الأرض إنا لفي خلق جديد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One grammatical account uses thumma for stages separated by a complete break, while fa marks the closer succession of clot-to-morsel, morsel-to-bones, and bones-to-flesh.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل في وجهه أن ما عطف بثم له بينونة كاملة مع ما عطف عليه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib traces tabāraka to baraka, permanence or settledness; baraka is enduring divine good within a thing, like water remaining in a pool.
rows.anchor: والبركة ثبوت الخير الإلهي في الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's tabāraka means He uniquely possesses abundant good and freely pours it upon creation; this good is realized through His measuring and bringing things into existence.
rows.anchor: فالتبارك منه تعالى اختصاصه بالخير الكثير الذي يجود به ويفيضه على خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because khalq originally means measuring and proportioning, God's arrangement of parts to fit one another and their surroundings generates abundant good.
rows.anchor: وهو إيجاد الأشياء وتركيب أجزائها بحيث تتناسب فيما بين أنفسها وتناسب ما وراءها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Best of creators” does not make creation exclusive to God: other beings also create in the sense of estimating or forming, a usage found elsewhere in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: ووصفه تعالى بأحسن الخالقين يدل على عدم اختصاص الخلق به وهو كذلك لما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These rulings continue the fitting sequence of legal instructions in the passage.
rows.anchor: بيان أحكام وشرائع متناسبة ومناسبة لما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uns means affinity and a settled heart; istiʾnās is seeking that familiarity by signaling—such as remembering God or clearing one's throat—so a householder knows someone wants to enter.
rows.anchor: الأنس بالشيء وإليه الإلفة وسكون القلب إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signal lets residents prepare before being seen in a private state; the rule protects their privacy and the dignity of faith.
rows.anchor: فربما كان في حال لا يحب أن يراه عليها أحد أو يطلع عليها مطلع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signaling before entry and then greeting the residents helps conceal private matters and reassures them that the visitor poses no threat.
rows.anchor: فأخبر باستيناسه صاحب البيت بدخوله ثم دخل فسلم عليه فقد أعانه على ستر عورته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maintaining this practice strengthens brotherhood, affection, and mutual cooperation in showing what is good and covering what is shameful, foundations of social happiness.
rows.anchor: ويؤدي الاستمرار على هذا السيرة الجميلة إلى استحكام الأخوة والإلفة والتعاون العام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's reminder points to the duties of preserving brotherhood and united hearts through which social well-being is sustained.
rows.anchor: أي لعلكم بالاستمرار على هذه السيرة تتذكرون ما يجب عليكم رعايته وإحياؤه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative supplies an omitted phrase: the rule was given so people would recall God's admonitions and act accordingly; the author allows this reading.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن قوله { لعلكم تذكرون } تعليل لمحذوف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A proposed transposition puts greeting before signaling; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects it.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن في قوله { حتى تستأنسوا وتسلموا } تقديما وتأخيرا

words: فَإِن لَّمْ تَجِدُوا۟ فِيهَآ أَحَدًۭا فَلَا تَدْخُلُوهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If no person with authority to admit the visitor is present, entry must await that person's permission; the clause does not license looking inside and entering if no one is seen, since the context bars looking at people's privacy.
rows.anchor: من قبل من يملك الإذن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding verse covers entry when the person authorized to admit is present and does not refuse; verse 28 covers houses with no such person present.
rows.anchor: والآية السابقة تبين حكم الدخول وفيه من يملك الإذن ولا يمنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A resident's refusal is treated by the following instruction to turn back, at 24:28.
rows.anchor: وأما دخوله وفيه من يملك الإذن ويمنع ولا يأذن فيه فيبين حكمه

words: بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ مَسْكُونَةٍ فِيهَا مَتَاعٌ لَّكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In them is enjoyment for you” is an adjective phrase describing the houses, not a separate explanatory sentence.
rows.anchor: ظاهر السياق كون قوله { فيها متاع لكم } صفة بعد صفة لقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matāʿ means use or enjoyment: entry is generally allowed in uninhabited facilities built for public use, such as inns, baths, and mills.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المتاع بمعنى الاستمتاع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes matāʿ as goods or merchandise and the houses as shops open to customers; the author finds this less likely because the wording is too narrow for that sense.
rows.anchor: وربما قيل إن المراد بالمتاع المعنى الاسمي وهو الأثاث والأشياء الموضوعة للبيع والشرى

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب الأنصاري
rows.claim: Asked what istiʾnās means, the Prophet says to announce oneself to the household with tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, takbīr, or throat-clearing; al-Durr al-manthūr also transmits this report.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أيوب الأنصاري قال قلنا يا رسول الله ما الاستيناس

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: When a man peered into one of the Prophet's chambers, the Prophet threatened to pierce his eye with a comb and explained that permission is required to prevent looking; al-Durr al-manthūr also transmits it.
rows.anchor: عن سهل بن سعد قال اطلع رجل في حجرة من حجر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A man asks whether he must seek permission to enter upon his mother each time; the Prophet asks whether he would want to see her naked, and he agrees permission is necessary.
rows.anchor: قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أستأذن على أمي؟ فقال نعم

rows.speaker: عمرو بن سعد الثقفي
rows.claim: After a visitor sought entry by clearing his throat, the Prophet had Rawḍa teach him to say “Peace be upon you; may I enter?”; al-Durr al-manthūr attributes this report to ʿAmr b. Saʿd al-Thaqafī.
rows.anchor: وروي أن رجلا استأذن على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم فتنحنح

rows.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh says that whoever lets his eye enter before asking permission and greeting has disobeyed God and has no permission.
rows.anchor: عن عبادة بن الصامت أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم سئل عن الاستيذان في البيوت
